name: Sinopia
lede: Sinopia is the red earth pigment of the Black Sea port of Sinope; painters later gave its name to the red underdrawing beneath a fresco, and heralds let it drift to green.

sections.title: The port and the name
sections.body:
*Sinopia* comes from Sinope, now Sinop on the Black Sea coast of Turkey, the port from which red ochre reached the Roman world [1][2][3]. Pastoureau says the Latin terms derived from its name all evoke the color red [2]. Finlay reports that the best of it was stamped with a seal and sold as "sealed Sinope" [1].

Ancient writers agree on its quality but not on where the best came from. Theophrastus says the pigment was named for the port it shipped from [4]. Strabo, in the first century BC, says the finest ruddle came from Cappadocia and was called Sinopean because merchants carried it down to Sinope, and he ranks it with the Iberian vermilion [4]. Vitruvius lists Sinope, Egypt, the Balearic Islands and Lemnos as sources of red earth [4]. Pliny implies that *rubrica* was a second-rate sinoper [4]. Pastoureau adds that the long sea voyage to the western ports made it expensive [5].

sections.title: What it was
sections.body:
Sinopia was a relatively pure, earthy iron oxide, the same family as hematite and [[ochre]] [4]. Dioscorides, the Greek physician of the first century, called it heavy and dense and likened it to the color of liver [6]. Paterson says the Greeks painted ships in sinopic red [3].

The swatch here is a hot red-orange [7]. That is brighter than a liver-brown earth, so treat it as a screen stand-in for the word, not a measurement of the ancient pigment [6][7].

Books disagree on what the names covered. Paterson says sinopia is sometimes called cinnabar [3], and the Pigment Compendium cites a medieval recipe filed under *synoper* that is clearly cinnabar, the mercury sulphide behind [[vermilion]] [4]. Church (1901) lists sinopia as another word for red ochre [4]. Paterson also lists it among the names of oxide reds sold by place, such as [[venetian-red]] and [[indian-red]] [3]. For *cinabrese*, Montagna (1993) is cited for a mixture of two parts sinopia to one of bianco sangiovanni used in fresco and tempera, while the Compendium elsewhere calls it sinoper mixed with calcium carbonate [4].

sections.title: The fresco drawing
sections.body:
In wall painting the word turned from a material into a drawing. A sinopia is the preliminary sketch in red on the first coat of plaster, and the Latin word survived into French and English with that meaning [5][2][3]. Pastoureau notes that the red ochre chalk gives effects like blood [2].

St Clair relates that in July 1944 a bullet set fire to a building beside the leaning tower in Pisa and damaged its Renaissance frescoes [6]. When the remains were taken off the walls for repair, many preparatory sinopia drawings were revealed beneath, and they can still be seen [6].

sections.title: From red to green in heraldry
sections.body: In heraldry the word *sinople* meant red until the fifteenth century and then green [3][8]. Pastoureau says it comes from the Latin *sinopia*, the red clay of the Sinop region, and long signified red before taking the sense of green [8]. His book on green takes up why [2]. Where a medieval source says *sinople*, check which color is meant before picturing red.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of color distance, in 60 paintings [9]. That is about a quarter of one per cent, and the match is as photographed: museum photographs of aged, varnished works, not a pigment test [9].

The best matches are Indian: the strongest is a page from a Basohli *Bhagavata Purana* of about 1760, where it fills 56 per cent of the picture [9]. Pahari painting carries it in 3 of 118 works, about ten times the archive rate [9]. By century the 1400s stand out at 8 of 945 paintings, about three times the archive rate [9]. The color most often seen beside it is [[rust]] [9].

questions.q: In fresco painting, what is a sinopia?
choices: A red preliminary drawing on the first coat of plaster
A green glaze laid over a finished wall
A kind of lime used to bind pigment
questions.answer: A red preliminary drawing on the first coat of plaster

questions.q: In heraldry, the word sinople, from a Latin word for a red clay, came to mean which color?

openers: Sinopia is both an ancient red earth from the port of Sinope and the red sketch hidden under a fresco [1][5].
In heraldry the word sinople came to mean green, though it long signified red; the reasons for the change are unknown [2][8].

issues: Heraldry: removed unsupported 'red until the fifteenth century' dating; Pastoureau says green from about 1350, Paterson differs; hedged
'His book on green takes up why' replaced: Pastoureau says the reasons are unknown
